The index has gone sideways for three months.

Most people see that as dead money.

William O'Neil saw it as the most important research window of the cycle.

While the market chops, the next leaders are quietly building bases. When the market turns, they are the first stocks out.

Here is what to look for:
- The stock is holding above its 50-day line while the index struggles
- Its relative strength line is at or near new highs, meaning it is outperforming a flat market
- It is forming a recognizable base near its highs: cup with handle, flat base, or double bottom
- Volume dries up inside the base. The sellers are running out.
- Earnings and sales growth are still accelerating underneath

Focusing on trimming to pay for risk is a foundational risk-management technique I use to systematically shift the odds in my favor. 

Here's how:

Eliminating Trade-Level Downside: 

By selling a portion of the position during the initial vertical expansion, you recover your initial dollar risk. This means the worst-case scenario for the remainder of the trade is reduced to zero.

Leveraging Market Momentum: 

Strong leading stocks don't move in a straight line; they pulse higher. Trimming into that vertical strength allows you to monetize the market's aggressive buying pressure rather than giving back unrealized gains during standard technical pullbacks.

Preserving Mental Capital and Removing Emotion: 

Carrying a full, heavy position through volatile tape creates psychological friction. When you know a trade is already "paid for," your emotional attachment drops. You stop micro-managing every tick and can patiently let the core position work.

Creating Asymmetric Payoffs: 

Taking partial profits while keeping a runner turns standard trades into asymmetric opportunities. You cap your initial downside through disciplined stops, but you keep your upside open-ended, maximizing your long-term expectancy.

On Iran

The same developments strengthening Iran’s bargaining position may also be creating an opening for China, and a politically useful exit for Trump.

Saudi Arabia’s East–West pipeline was shut after a drone attack originating from Iraq. A critical route designed to bypass Hormuz has itself proved vulnerable. Separately, the Iran-aligned Houthis seized Perim island at Bab el-Mandeb, strengthening their position around the Red Sea’s southern entrance. 

Saudi Arabia asked Washington for direct military help against the Houthis. Trump declined, although intelligence support continues. 

This is not complete abandonment, but it will probably feel like it to the Saudis and demonstrates a limit to the additional fighting Washington is willing to undertake. 

My read: Iran’s leverage has increased, while the Gulf states have more reason to question whether relying on American protection alone can secure their infrastructure and exports. That creates pressure to negotiate, not necessarily because they trust Tehran, but because the alternatives are becoming more costly. 

China is an important part of this equation.

Hormuz matters for its Gulf energy supplies. Bab el-Mandeb matters for the Asia–Europe shipping route through Suez, as well as Red Sea oil shipments heading towards Asia. Disruption at both therefore threatens different parts of China’s economy: energy supplies on one side, trade routes on the other. 

This does not mean Chinese trade stops. Ships can divert around Africa, and many already have. But longer journeys and higher transport costs are still an economic penalty, a costly solution with consequences. 

The cost is already visible: Reuters reported this week that the Gulf of Oman–China supertanker freight benchmark reached roughly $11.50 per barrel, its highest since that benchmark launched earlier this year. 

Beijing also has economic leverage with Tehran. China bought more than 80% of Iran’s seaborne oil exports in 2025, according to Kpler data cited by Reuters. That gives it an important relationship through which to press for accommodation, though economic leverage is not the same as control over Iran or the Houthis. 

The diplomacy is worth watching.

On September 8, Wang Yi discussed energy and shipping security with Qatar’s prime minister. China’s official readout described Qatari support for closer coordination and a more independent regional security framework. Today, September 12, Xi urged BRICS to take a peacemaking role in the conflict. 

My interpretation is that Beijing has both an economic incentive to stabilise the region and an opportunity to gain influence by helping regional governments reach an accommodation. It does not need to replace the American military to become more important diplomatically.

That is the possibility I would watch around the proposed Oman talks: a settlement that improves shipping and regional security while reducing Washington’s freedom of action.

Restrictions on using Gulf territory, airspace or American facilities for attacks on Iran could conceivably become part of a broader bargain. Those are possible future concessions, not confirmed terms of Monday’s discussions. I would put more weight on gradual restrictions and diversified partnerships than on Gulf states collectively expelling US forces.

For Trump, that could create an unusual outcome: a strategic setback that still offers a political exit.

November’s midterms are approaching, while energy-driven inflation and pressure for higher interest rates are increasing the domestic cost of the conflict. A credible improvement in energy flows would address part of that pressure, without guaranteeing lower rates. 

A Gulf-led agreement could let Trump argue that regional governments chose their own accommodation with Iran, so America should not expand the war on their behalf. He could place responsibility for the concessions on those governments while presenting reduced US involvement as respecting their decision.

That is a possible political narrative that is building.

The incentives could align: Iran obtains concessions, Gulf states gain more reliable security and exports, China protects trade and gains diplomatic standing, and Trump gets a way to step back. All different shades of a win, some politically, others through power and yet others through money.

But aligned incentives are not agreed terms. Bahrain says it will not attend meetings with Iran, Oman reportedly rejects Tehran’s proposed shipping fees, and a senior Iranian official says no signed Hormuz agreement is expected on Monday. This is not yet a united regional settlement. 

Nor can Washington simply be removed from the equation: Iran’s stated position still makes reopening conditional on US concessions. 

The opportunity is not “China takes over and America disappears.” It is that a less US-centred regional arrangement could simultaneously give China influence, give Trump an exit, and give markets relief.

Those outcomes are not mutually exclusive, I’m mostly pointing out that there is path to regional deescalation that indirectly help the US through lower oil prices and through it yields.
